'''''Prunus mahaleb''''', the '''St Lucie cherry''' or '''mahaleb cherry''', is a species of [[cherry]], native to central and southern Europe, northwest Africa, southwest Asia, and parts of central Asia.<ref name=IUCN/><ref name=empp>Euro+Med Plantbase Project: [http://ww2.bgbm.org/_EuroPlusMed/PTaxonDetail.asp?NameId=29650&PTRefFk=500000 ''Prunus mahaleb''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928003818/http://ww2.bgbm.org/_EuroPlusMed/PTaxonDetail.asp?NameId=29650&PTRefFk=500000 |date=2007-09-28 }}</ref><ref name="Rushforth">{{cite book | last=Rushforth | first=Keith | title=Trees of Britain and Europe | publisher=Trafalgar Square Publishing | publication-place=London | date=1999 | isbn=0-00-220013-9 | pages=1023–1024}}</ref><ref name="PlantAtlas">{{cite web | title=St Lucie Cherry ''Prunus mahaleb'' L. | website=PlantAtlas | url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.qg6 | access-date=2026-02-06}}</ref> The tree is cultivated for a spice obtained from the seeds inside the cherry stones. The seeds have a fragrant scent and have a taste comparable to bitter almonds with cherry notes.

==Description==
[[File:Korina 2012-07-17 Prunus mahaleb 1.jpg|thumb|left|St Lucie cherry fruit, Germany]]
It is a [[deciduous]] [[tree]] or large [[shrub]], growing to 2–10 m (rarely up to 12 m) tall with a trunk up to 40 cm diameter. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is grey-brown, with conspicuous [[lenticel]]s on young stems, and shallowly fissured on old trunks. The [[leaves]] are {{Convert|1.5–5|cm|abbr=off|frac=4}} long, 1–4 cm. wide, alternate, clustered at the end of alternately arranged twigs, ovate to cordate, pointed, have serrate edges, longitudinal venation and are [[glabrousness (botany)|glabrous]] and green. The [[petiole (botany)|petiole]] is 5–20 millimetres long, and may or may not have two glands. The [[flower]]s are fragrant, pure white, small, 8–20 mm diameter, with an 8–15 mm [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]]; they are arranged 3–10 together on a 3–4 cm long [[raceme]]. The flower [[pollination]] is mainly by [[bee]]s. The [[fruit]] is a small thin-fleshed cherry-like [[drupe]] 8–10 mm in diameter, green at first, turning red then dark purple to black when mature, with a very bitter flavour; flowering is in mid spring with the fruit ripening in mid to late summer.<ref name="Rushforth"/><ref name=fnwe>Flora of NW Europe: [http://ip30.eti.uva.nl/BIS/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=2717 ''Prunus mahaleb''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071215005725/http://ip30.eti.uva.nl/BIS/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=2717 |date=2007-12-15 }}</ref><ref name=blamey>Blamey, M. & Grey-Wilson, C. (1989). ''Flora of Britain and Northern Europe''. {{ISBN|0-340-40170-2}}.</ref>

It demonstrates selective fruit abortion, producing a high proportion of excess flowers that result in low fruit set levels. This reduces the number of "poor quality" fruit and increases the viability of its seeds.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1002/j.1537-2197.1993.tb15369.x | title=Why ''Prunus mahaleb'' (Rosaceae) produces more flowers than fruits | year=1993 | last1=Guitian | first1=Javier | journal=American Journal of Botany | volume=80 | issue=11 | pages=1305–1309 |jstor=2445715 | bibcode=1993AmJB...80.1305G }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1002/j.1537-2197.1994.tb11466.x | title=Selective fruit abortion in ''Prunus mahaleb'' (Rosaceae) | year=1994 | last1=Guitian | first1=Javier | journal=American Journal of Botany | volume=81 | issue=12 | pages=1555–1558 |jstor=2445332 | bibcode=1994AmJB...81.1555G }}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
[[File:Prunus mahaleb sl17.jpg|left|thumb|Plants in flower in native habitat, Mödlinger Klause, [[Mödling District]], Lower Austria]]
''Prunus mahaleb'' occurs in thickets and open woodland on dry slopes; in central Europe at altitudes up to {{Convert|1,700|m|abbr=on}}, and in highlands at 1,200–2,000 m in southern Europe.<ref name="blamey" /> It has become [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in some temperate areas, including Europe north of its native range (north to [[Great Britain]] and [[Sweden]]), and locally in [[Australia]] and the United States.<ref name="blamey" /><ref>New South Wales Flora: [http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Prunus~mahaleb ''Prunus mahaleb'']</ref><ref>USDA Plants Profile: [https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=PRMA ''Prunus mahaleb'']</ref> mahaleb cherry<ref>{{PLANTS|id=PRMA|taxon=Prunus mahaleb|access-date=14 October 2015}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
A scientific study<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.2307/2937263 | title=''Prunus mahaleb'' and Birds: The High-efficiency Seed Dispersal System of a Temperate Fruiting Tree | last1=Herrera | first1=Carlos M. | last2=Jordano | first2=Pedro | journal=Ecological Monographs | year=1981 | volume=51 | issue=2 | pages=203–218 | hdl=10261/45070 |jstor=2937263| bibcode=1981EcoM...51..203H | url=http://digital.csic.es/bitstream/10261/45070/1/HJ_1981_EcolMonogrHQ.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200711000458/http://digital.csic.es/bitstream/10261/45070/1/HJ_1981_EcolMonogrHQ.pdf| archive-date=2020-07-11|url-status=live }}</ref> discovered an ecological dependence between the plant and four species of frugivorous birds in southeastern [[Spain]]; [[Common blackbird|blackbird]]s and [[blackcap]]s proved to be the most important seed dispersers. When ''P. mahaleb'' is fruiting, these birds consume the fruit almost exclusively, and disperse the seeds to the locations favourable for the tree's growth. The way in which some birds consume the fruit, and the habitats those birds use, may act as a selective force in determining which genetic variations of the cherry flourish.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.2307/3545521 | jstor=3545521 | title=Spatial Variation in the Interactions between ''Prunus mahaleb'' and Frugivorous Birds | last1=Guitián | first1=José | last2=Fuentes | first2=Marcelino | last3=Bermejo | first3=Teresa | last4=López | first4=Belén | journal=Oikos | year=1992 | volume=63 | issue=1 | pages=125–130 | bibcode=1992Oikos..63..125G }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
Away from its native range, the species is grown as an [[ornamental tree]] for its strongly fragrant flowers, throughout temperate regions of the world. A number of [[cultivar]]s have been selected for their ornamental value, including 'Albomarginata', with [[variegation|variegated]] foliage, 'Bommii', a dwarf with strongly pendulous branches, 'Globosa', a compact dwarf clone, 'Pendula', with drooping branching, and 'Xanthocarpa' with yellow fruit.<ref name="bean">Bean, W. J. (1976). ''Trees and Shrubs Hardy in the British Isles''. John Murray {{ISBN|0-7195-2427-X}}.</ref> It has also been used as a [[rootstock]] for grafting other cherries on.<ref name="PlantAtlas"/>

==Uses==
[[File:Przekrój Prunus mahaleb Wiśnia wonna OB UWr 2023-07-21 01.jpg|thumb|right|Crosscut wood of St Lucie cherry]]
The plant is also cultivated for [[mahleb]], a spice obtained from the seeds inside the cherry stones. It is fragrant and has the taste of bitter [[almond]]s.<ref name=GernotKatzersSpicePages>Gernot Katzer's Spice Pages: [http://gernot-katzers-spice-pages.com/engl/Prun_mah.html Mahaleb Cherry (''Prunus mahaleb'' L.)]</ref> It is used in small quantities to sharpen sweet foods, such as the [[Turkish cuisine|Turkish]] sweet-bread [[çörek]] (chorak), the [[Greece|Greek]] sweet-bread [[tsoureki]] or the [[Armenia]]n sweet-bread chorak. The chemical constituents are still uncertain, but the spice is prepared from the seeds, either by grinding and powdering the seed kernels, or in oil extracted from the seeds.<ref name=GernotKatzersSpicePages/>

The [[wood]] is hard, and is used in cabinet-making and for [[smoking pipe (tobacco)|pipes]].<ref name=vedel>Vedel, H., & Lange, J. (1960). ''Trees and Bushes in Wood and Hedgerow''. Metheun & Co. Ltd., London.</ref>

The bark, wood, and seeds contain [[coumarin]].<ref name=vedel/><ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1002/jps.2600590424 | title=Some Coumarin Constituents of ''Prunus mahaleb'' L. Fruit Kernels V | year=1970 | last1=El-Dakhakhny | first1=M. | journal=Journal of Pharmaceutical Sciences | volume=59 | issue=4 | pages=551–553 | pmid=5440687 | bibcode=1970JPhmS..59..551E }}</ref> They have anti-inflammatory, sedative and vasodilation effects.{{Citation needed|date=May 2021|reason=No source is given for these claims.}}

==History==
{{main|Mahleb}}

''Prunus mahaleb'' is a likely candidate for the ḫalub-tree mentioned in early Sumerian writings, a durable fruit-bearing hardwood with seeds and leaves known for their medicinal properties and associated with the goddess [[Inana]].<ref>Gadotti, A. (2014). Gilgamesh, Enkidu, and the Netherworld and the Sumerian Gilgamesh Cycle. De Gruyter. {{ISBN|161451545X}}.</ref> The Arabic {{lang|ar|محلب}} ''mahleb'' or ''mahlab'' meaning the mahaleb cherry is in medieval Islamic writings by among others [[Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi|Al-Razi]] (died 925 or 932), [[Ibn al-Baitar]] (died 1248) and [[Ibn al-Awwam]].<ref>"Mahaleb" in [https://archive.org/stream/remarquessurlesm00lammuoft#page/151/mode/1up ''Remarques sur les mots français dérivés de l'arabe''], by [[Henri Lammens]], year 1890.</ref> Ibn Al-Awwam in his book on agriculture dated late 12th century described how to cultivate the mahaleb tree: he says the tree is a vigorous grower, easy to grow, but a thing to watch out for is that it is not resistant to prolonged drought. He also described how to prepare the mahaleb seeds by boiling them in sugared water.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=PuEOAAAAQAAJ&q=mahaleb&pg=PA367 ''Le livre de l'agriculture''], by Ibn al-'Awwam, translated to French J.-J. Clément-Mullet, year 1866, volume II page 367–368.</ref> The word, and probably the mahaleb itself, does not appear in classical Latin, nor early or mid medieval Latin, and is rare in late medieval Latin. One early record in Latin is year 1317 in an encyclopedia by [[Matthaeus Silvaticus]] who wrote that the "''mahaleb''" is the kernel seed of the fruit of both domesticated and wild cherry trees in Arabic countries.<ref>"Maaleb" and "mahaleb" in the [http://daten.digitale-sammlungen.de/bsb00060733/image_315 ''Pandectarum'' of Matthaeus Silvaticus] (in Latin).</ref> Another early record in Latin is in a medical-botany book by Ioannis Mesuae in 1479 spelled ''almahaleb'' (where ''"[[al-]]"'' is the Arabic definite article).<ref name=CNRTL /> In 1593 the Latin botanist [[Carolus Clusius]] spelled it ''mahaleb''.<ref name=CNRTL>[http://www.cnrtl.fr/lexicographie/mahaleb ''Mahaleb'' @ CNRTL.fr] (in French).</ref> Today its cultivation and use is largely restricted to the region that in the 19th and earlier centuries formed the [[Ottoman Empire]]. Syria is the main exporting country.<ref name=GernotKatzersSpicePages />
